clue.text: People have to affirm ties?

parts.note: people in general, as in 'all men'
to affirm something solemnly is to swear it

explanation.surface: People are required to declare something about their neckties, or perhaps confirm a draw.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a definition by example: ties are one kind of the clothing in question.
explanation.definitionFit: Neckties are an example of clothing sold for men, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Cockney fellow's involved in this argument

indicators.note: something involved in another thing is wrapped up inside it

parts.note: taken as written; the outer word
'he's' with the H dropped, as a Cockney says it: 'e's

explanation.surface: A Londoner is caught up in this particular dispute.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockneys famously drop their aitches, so 'he's' becomes 'e's, which sits inside THIS.
explanation.definitionFit: A thesis is a proposition put forward and argued for, so it is an argument.

clue.text: Socialist has to abandon town

parts.note: red is the colour of socialism
to ditch something is to abandon it

explanation.surface: A left-winger is forced to leave some town behind.
explanation.walkthrough: Redditch is a town in Worcestershire, in the English Midlands.
explanation.definitionFit: Redditch is a specific English town, south of Birmingham, so 'town' is a definition by category.

clue.text: Broken elbow initially restricted Harmison, perhaps

indicators.note: something broken is smashed apart and its pieces can be put back in another order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letter of the word that follows it

parts.note: the first letter of restricted

explanation.surface: An injured elbow at first limited the England fast man Steve Harmison.
explanation.walkthrough: Steve Harmison was an England fast bowler of the 2000s; a cricket injury fits the surface perfectly.
explanation.definitionFit: Harmison is an example of a cricketer who delivers the ball, hence 'perhaps' marking a definition by example.

clue.text: Simmer or boil these with a little eggplant

indicators.note: things set to boil churn about, so the letters are stirred into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: a little of the word means just its first letter is used

parts.note: the first letter of eggplant

explanation.surface: A recipe instruction: simmer or boil these vegetables with a bit of aubergine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Simmer or boil' reads as a single cooking instruction, but only 'Simmer' defines; 'boil' stirs the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To seethe is to simmer with barely suppressed anger, as liquid does just below boiling.

clue.text: Prisoner gets away from policeman fast

indicators.note: something that gets away from a thing leaves it, so it is taken out of that word

parts.note: a constable is a police officer
a con is a convict

explanation.surface: A convict quickly escapes from the officer guarding him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fast' looks like 'quickly', but here it means firmly fixed, as in 'stuck fast'. CONSTABLE without CON leaves STABLE.
explanation.definitionFit: Fast in the sense of firmly fixed or secure is a synonym of steady and immovable.

clue.text: Express need to be different

indicators.note: becoming different means taking a new form, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written; it also helps form the indicator phrase

explanation.surface: A plea to state openly the desire to stand out from the crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to' does double duty here, both as fodder and as part of the anagram phrase; NEED and TO rearrange to the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To denote is to signify or indicate, which is a way of expressing a meaning.

clue.text: Wandering rough terrain one gets lost

indicators.note: rough suggests a rugged, disordered state, so the letters are jumbled
when something gets lost it disappears, so a letter drops out

parts.note: taken as written
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A hiker roaming over rough ground loses their way.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the I out of TERRAIN and rearrange what is left.
explanation.definitionFit: Errant means straying or travelling about, as a knight errant roams in search of adventure.

clue.text: Italian politician reviewed prom on radio

indicators.note: something reviewed is gone over again and reworked, so the letters are reorganised

parts.note: the letters of all three words

explanation.surface: An Italian statesman critiqued a broadcast of a promenade concert.
explanation.walkthrough: The Proms are a famous summer series of classical concerts in London, broadcast on BBC radio.
explanation.definitionFit: Romano Prodi was Prime Minister of Italy and President of the European Commission.

clue.text: Two leaders leave one state for another

indicators.note: when the leaders leave, the two letters at the front are dropped

parts.note: a southern US state

explanation.surface: Two bosses quit one US state to move to a different one.
explanation.walkthrough: The state is found by trying US state names that keep working after the front two letters go: ARKANSAS loses AR.
explanation.definitionFit: Kansas is a US state other than the first one, so 'another' stands for a different state.

clue.text: Veteran to honour the Stars and Stripes

parts.note: a veteran is old, experienced
glory is honour or renown

explanation.surface: An old soldier salutes the American flag.
explanation.definitionFit: Old Glory is a long-standing nickname for the national flag of the United States.

clue.text: Conservative spent a lot of money, we hear

indicators.note: what we hear is a sound, so the answer sounds like the word clued

parts.note: to blow money is to spend it lavishly

explanation.surface: Gossip about a Tory who went on a spending spree.
explanation.walkthrough: Blue is the party colour of Britain's Conservatives, so a Tory is a blue.
explanation.definitionFit: In British politics a Conservative supporter is called a blue, after the party's colour.

clue.text: Dash to make confession about affair

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one word goes round the other

parts.note: to sing is slang for confessing to the police
an affair is a matter or business

explanation.surface: Someone rushes to admit to an extramarital fling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Confession' stands for the verb sing, as when a suspect sings to the police; 'Dash' is a small amount, not a rush.
explanation.definitionFit: A dash is a small quantity added, just as a smattering is a slight amount.

clue.text: Batsman's smashing cricket shot

indicators.note: smashing something breaks it into pieces that can be rearranged

parts.note: the letters of both words

explanation.surface: A batsman plays a hard-hit stroke on the cricket field.
explanation.walkthrough: Marcus Trescothick was an England opening batsman of the 2000s. 'Batsman's' is 'Batsman is', with 'smashing' the anagram signal rather than praise.
explanation.definitionFit: Trescothick was a left-handed opening batter for Somerset and England, so he is an example of a batsman.

clue.text: Nietzschean hero or comic character?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the ideal superior being in Nietzsche's philosophy, the Übermensch
second meaning: the caped hero of the DC comic books

explanation.walkthrough: The English translation of Nietzsche's Übermensch shares its name with the comic-book hero.
explanation.definitionFit: The word translates the philosopher's ideal being and is also the name of a famous comic-strip protagonist.

clue.text: General acceptance of money

definitions.meaning: first meaning: being widely accepted, as an idea that gains wide use
second meaning: the coins and notes used in a country

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests money being accepted everywhere; the word means both wide circulation of ideas and cash itself.
explanation.definitionFit: The word covers both cash in circulation and the state of being widely accepted or used.

clue.text: Supporting the French workers

parts.note: pro means in favour of
les is the French plural 'the'

explanation.surface: Backing the labourers of France.
explanation.definitionFit: Proles is an informal word, from Orwell's 1984, for the working classes.

clue.text: Is ultimately not as high and not as fast

indicators.note: ultimately points to the very end, so only the closing letter is taken

parts.note: the last letter of Is
less high is lower

explanation.surface: A comparison: something is in the end less lofty and less speedy.
explanation.definitionFit: Slower is the comparative of slow, meaning having less speed.

clue.text: Environmentalists have naive side

parts.note: green means inexperienced or naive
a party is one side in a dispute or contract

explanation.surface: Eco-campaigners are said to have a gullible streak.
explanation.definitionFit: The Green Party is a political party made up of environmental campaigners.

clue.text: Old flame's name causing upset

parts.note: an ex is a former partner; the 's is 'has'
to cite is to name, as a source or a person in court

explanation.surface: Hearing a former lover's name mentioned brings on distress.
explanation.definitionFit: To excite is to agitate or stir up, a near synonym of upset used as a verb.

clue.text: One may become a farmer

indicators.note: may become signals a change of form, so the letters turn into something new

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written; it also helps form the indicator phrase

explanation.surface: A general remark that anyone might go on to work the land.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole thing reads like a proverb, but ONE and MAY are themselves the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A yeoman was historically a man owning and cultivating a small landed estate, a freeholding farmer.

clue.text: Releasing a thousand tiny shrimps in stream

indicators.note: releasing something lets it go, so it is removed from the word

parts.note: krill are small shrimp-like crustaceans
K is the abbreviation for a thousand

explanation.surface: Letting a thousand tiny shrimps go free into a brook.
explanation.definitionFit: A rill is a small brook or rivulet, so it is a little stream.

clue.text: Gloomy chap's a parliamentary official

parts.note: a black mood is a gloomy one
Rod is a man's name, standing for any chap

explanation.surface: A morose man works as a functionary at Westminster.
explanation.walkthrough: Black Rod is the House of Lords officer who knocks on the Commons door at the State Opening of Parliament.
explanation.definitionFit: Black Rod is the title of a senior ceremonial officer of the UK House of Lords.

clue.text: I take a couple of punches

definitions.note: the answer is a single combination of two punches, the clue's plural noun

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
a couple is two

explanation.surface: A boxer admits to being hit a couple of times.
explanation.walkthrough: In boxing a one-two is a quick jab followed by a stronger punch with the other hand.
explanation.definitionFit: A one-two is a boxing combination of two rapid blows, left then right.

clue.text: Governor's one gin

parts.note: the S of the possessive, taken as written
a means one
a gin is a snare for catching animals

explanation.surface: The governor owns a single bottle of spirit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gin' looks like the drink but is the trap for game. A satrap was a provincial governor in ancient Persia.
explanation.definitionFit: A satrap was the governor of a province in the ancient Persian Empire.

clue.text: Craned awkwardly to see Nureyev?

indicators.note: doing something awkwardly means it comes out clumsily ordered, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An audience member stretched their neck uncomfortably to glimpse the great ballet star.
explanation.walkthrough: Rudolf Nureyev was a famous Soviet-born ballet star; the question mark marks him as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Nureyev is an example of a ballet performer, hence the question mark.
